rationale: Start with a broad mid-length scouting gradient spanning the full practical solvent range to reveal the retention spread of all 10 compounds and identify whether the mixture is generally too retained, too unretained, or well distributed. A moderate temperature gives a balanced first map without biasing strongly toward either extreme selectivity regime.

All 10 compounds eluted with excellent resolution, so the only clear opportunity is to reduce analysis time while preserving the still-comfortable minimum resolution around peaks 6–7. A shorter full-range gradient should compress the chromatogram and improve the time term without likely pushing the current worst pair anywhere near co-elution.

At 12 min the run became very fast but over-compressed the critical 6/7 pair, so a small increase in gradient time is the most direct way to recover full resolution while likely keeping the time penalty at zero. This brackets the optimum between 12 and 20 min and should move the method closer to the best CRF.

The critical pair improved substantially from 12 to 14 min but is still the only sub-1.5 pair, so another small increase in gradient time is the safest way to target full resolution while likely remaining in the zero time-penalty region. This should place the optimum very near 16 min if resolution continues to scale smoothly.

The optimum in gradient time appears near 14–16 min, and 14 min is currently best but limited by the 6/7 pair; changing temperature is the next efficient lever to alter selectivity without adding much run time. A modest decrease to 35 C may improve that critical separation while keeping the method in the fast, zero-time-penalty region.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by creating a new 5/6 coelution, so the next informative move is the opposite direction at the currently best gradient time. A modest increase to 45 C may improve the crowded mid-cluster selectivity enough to lift the 6/7 pair above 1.5 while keeping the run fast.

Since temperature did not help, the next targeted lever is to slightly raise the starting organic fraction to reshape the early-to-mid gradient profile and potentially decompress the crowded central cluster around peaks 5–7. Keeping tG at the current best 14 min preserves the favorable speed while probing selectivity in a different way than simply lengthening the gradient.

Raising phi0 improved both speed and CRF at 14 min, so the next logical move is a small increase in gradient time under this better selectivity regime to push the remaining critical 6/7 pair above 1.5. This should test whether the phi0 adjustment plus slightly gentler slope can deliver full resolution with only a minimal time cost.

The current method is nearly ideal, so only a very small time gain is left; lowering phi1 slightly may retain enough resolving power while reducing the effective gradient strength late in the run and subtly reshaping the crowded region. This is a low-risk local optimization around the best condition rather than a broad exploratory move.

The best method is essentially solved, so the remaining opportunity is a tiny reduction in run time while preserving full resolution; increasing phi0 further is the most plausible way to shift all peaks earlier. Because phi0 = 0.10 already improved CRF versus 0.05 at the same tG, testing 0.15 is a focused local step around the current optimum.

CRF has already reached the maximum, so this run is only to probe the robustness boundary and see whether still higher starting organic can preserve full resolution while keeping the method equally fast. It is the most direct local follow-up to the successful shift from phi0 0.10 to 0.15.

Since phi0 0.20 over-compressed the critical pair, the best region is likely centered at phi0 0.15; the remaining question is whether a shorter gradient can still maintain full resolution and match the maximum CRF. Testing 14 min at this improved starting composition probes the fastest potentially perfect method near the current optimum.

The optimum is already achieved, so this run is to map robustness on the slower side of the current best condition and confirm whether 16 min is the shortest fully optimal gradient at phi0 0.15. A slightly longer gradient should keep full resolution and reveal how sharply CRF falls once the time penalty increases.

With the optimum already found, the only meaningful nearby dimension not yet paired with phi0 0.15 is a slightly lower phi1 to test whether the same full resolution can be maintained with a different late-gradient shape. This checks robustness of the perfect method to endpoint changes and may reveal whether phi1 0.95 is uniquely favorable.

With a perfect CRF already secured, the best use of another injection is robustness mapping in a new dimension around the optimum. A small temperature decrease will show how sensitive the full-resolution optimum is to routine operating variation and whether 40 C sits at a selectivity sweet spot.

The drop at 35 C shows the optimum is temperature-sensitive, so the symmetric check at 45 C will complete the local robustness picture around the perfect method. This determines whether 40 C is a narrow selectivity maximum or whether higher temperature remains acceptable.

The maximum score is already achieved, so a sensible final local check is a stronger reduction in phi1 at the optimum phi0, tG, and T to define how much endpoint flexibility exists before time performance degrades. This extends the robustness map along the phi1 axis more meaningfully than repeating small temperature changes that already proved unfavorable.

The optimum has been found, so another useful point is the slower-side robustness limit at the same selectivity, extending the tG map beyond 18 min for the best phi0. This confirms the time-penalty trend around the maximum and better defines the local response surface near the chosen final method.

The best method is already known, so a higher-temperature stress point is useful to complete the robustness map beyond the 45 C check and show how rapidly selectivity collapses above the optimum. This is more informative now than further time or phi1 changes, which already showed only monotonic deterioration from the maximum.

We have mapped 35–50 C around the optimum and seen strong temperature sensitivity, so adding 30 C completes the lower-temperature side and defines the practical operating window around the perfect method. This is a more informative remaining point than more changes in phi1 or tG, which already showed only decline away from the optimum.

The optimum is already secured, so one remaining informative experiment is to define the upper phi0 robustness limit beyond the decline seen at 0.20. Testing 0.25 at the otherwise optimal settings will show how quickly the critical pair compresses as the starting organic fraction is pushed higher.

The upper phi0 limit is now clearly defined, so a useful remaining point is the shorter-gradient boundary at the optimal phi0 to quantify how much speed can be gained before the critical pair fails. This complements the 14 and 16 min data and sharpens the local process window around the best method.

With the optimal method already identified, one remaining informative robustness point is the lowest allowed temperature to complete the full temperature response around that optimum. This defines the extreme lower-temperature failure mode and finalizes the practical operating window more cleanly than additional composition variations.

The optimum is already established, and the last unmapped temperature extreme is 60 C; running it completes the full allowed temperature robustness profile around the best method. This gives the most additional information with one of the final injections by defining the upper operational failure boundary.

A nearby nonidentical condition is most useful for a final robustness check, and this combines the two modest shifts that were each individually close to optimal. It should remain fully resolved or nearly so while testing whether a slightly weaker, shorter gradient can match the best region without repeating a prior method.
